board_events.text: A wave carries energy and momentum through a medium with NO net transport of the medium itself.
A twig on a pond bobs up and down; it is not carried to the shore.
Each particle does its own small oscillation about a fixed mean position.
What we call 'the wave moving' is the phase of that oscillation, handed from particle to particle, slightly delayed.
Wave speed is set by the medium, not by how hard or fast you drive the source.
Louder or higher-pitched does NOT make the wave travel faster in the same medium.

segments.text: <curious>Have you ever watched a wave ripple around a packed stadium? One person stands and sits, then the next, then the next, and a giant ripple sweeps all the way around.
Here is the beautiful part. Not one person actually travelled around the stadium. Each stayed in their own seat. What moved was the pattern, the disturbance.
That is a wave in one sentence. It is a disturbance that travels through a medium, carrying energy and momentum from place to place, with no net transport of the medium itself.

Drop a pebble in a still pond and a floating twig just bobs up and down. It is not carried to the shore, even though the ripple clearly races outward. The water goes up and down; the energy goes outward.
Every particle of the medium is doing its own tiny oscillation about a fixed average position. Nobody leaves home.
So what does the wave moving really mean? It is the phase of that oscillation being handed from one particle to the next, each a little delayed, exactly like the stand-up cue passing down the row.
And here is a fact examiners love. The wave speed is fixed by the medium, not by how you produced the wave.
<whisper>Shouting louder or at a higher pitch will not make sound travel one bit faster through the same air.</whisper> Amplitude and frequency do not touch the speed.
<curious>कभी stadium में wave देखी है? एक इंसान खड़ा होकर बैठता है, फिर अगला, फिर अगला, और एक बड़ी ripple पूरे stadium में घूम जाती है।
पर मज़े की बात — कोई भी इंसान actually पूरे stadium में घूमा नहीं। हर कोई अपनी seat पर ही रहा। जो move हुआ वो था pattern, यानी disturbance।
यही है wave की definition। Wave एक disturbance है जो medium से travel करती है, energy और momentum को एक जगह से दूसरी जगह ले जाती है, बिना medium को खुद transport किए।
Pond में pebble डालो तो पास तैरता twig बस ऊपर-नीचे bob करता है, shore तक नहीं जाता, जबकि ripple बाहर की तरफ़ दौड़ती है। Water ऊपर-नीचे, energy बाहर।
Medium का हर particle अपनी fixed mean position के around एक छोटा सा oscillation कर रहा है। कोई अपनी जगह छोड़ता नहीं।
तो wave move करने का मतलब क्या? उस oscillation का phase एक particle से अगले particle को pass होता है, थोड़ा-थोड़ा delayed, बिल्कुल उस stand-up cue की तरह।
और ये point examiners को बहुत पसंद है — wave speed medium से तय होती है, इस बात से नहीं कि तुमने wave कैसे बनाई।
<whisper>ज़ोर से चिल्लाने या ऊँची pitch से sound उसी air में ज़रा भी तेज़ नहीं चलेगी।</whisper> Amplitude और frequency speed को छूते तक नहीं।

sections.title: Classifying waves and the five characteristics

board_events.text: How we classify waves - three cuts
Cut one, by medium: mechanical waves need matter (sound, string, water); electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays) travel through vacuum.
No medium, no sound - that is why space is silent.
Cut two: direction of vibration

board_events.caption: Transverse vs longitudinal motion

board_events.text: Transverse: particles move perpendicular to travel (rope, light, water). Longitudinal: particles move along travel, making compressions and rarefactions (sound).
Cut three, by dimensionality: a string wave is 1-D, pond ripples 2-D, firecracker sound 3-D.
Every wave shares five characteristics: amplitude, wavelength, time period, frequency, and wave speed.

segments.text: With so many kinds of waves, we need a way to sort them. There are three clean cuts, and every wave in your syllabus falls neatly into all three.

Cut one is about the medium. Mechanical waves need matter to move through: sound, a string, water ripples. Electromagnetic waves, light, radio, X-rays, need nothing at all and sail through empty vacuum.
That is exactly why space is silent. There is no air out there to carry a compression, so a scream in a vacuum makes literally no sound.
Cut two sorts waves by the direction the particles vibrate. This is the distinction the diagram makes crisp.

On the left, a transverse wave: each particle swings perpendicular to the direction of travel, like flicking a long rope up and down while the wave races sideways. On the right, a longitudinal wave: particles shuffle back and forth along the travel line, bunching into compressions and thinning into rarefactions, exactly like pushing and pulling a slinky.
So the rule of thumb is simple. Rope, light, and water ripples are transverse; sound is the classic longitudinal wave.
Cut three is dimensionality. A wave on a string spreads in one dimension, ripples on a pond in two, and sound from a firecracker in all three.
And no matter which boxes a wave lands in, the same five numbers describe it: amplitude, wavelength, time period, frequency, and wave speed.
इतनी सारी waves हैं, तो इन्हें sort कैसे करें? तीन साफ़ cuts हैं, और syllabus की हर wave तीनों में fit हो जाती है।

पहला cut medium का है। Mechanical waves को travel करने के लिए matter चाहिए — sound, string, water ripples। Electromagnetic waves जैसे light, radio, X-rays को कुछ नहीं चाहिए, ये खाली vacuum में भी चलती हैं।
इसीलिए space silent है। वहाँ air है ही नहीं जो compression carry करे, तो vacuum में चीख का कोई sound नहीं बनता।
दूसरा cut particles के vibrate करने की direction पर है। यही distinction diagram साफ़ करता है।

बाईं तरफ़ transverse wave — हर particle travel की direction के perpendicular झूलता है, जैसे लंबी rope को ऊपर-नीचे flick करना जबकि wave बग़ल में दौड़े। दाईं तरफ़ longitudinal wave — particles travel line के साथ आगे-पीछे होते हैं, compressions में बंधते और rarefactions में फैलते, बिल्कुल slinky push-pull की तरह।
तो simple rule — rope, light, water ripples transverse हैं; sound classic longitudinal wave है।
तीसरा cut dimensionality का है। String पर wave one dimension में फैलती है, pond की ripples two में, और firecracker की sound तीनों dimensions में।
और wave किन्हीं भी boxes में जाए, वही पाँच numbers उसे describe करते हैं: amplitude, wavelength, time period, frequency, और wave speed।

board_events.text: Trick: ride along with the pulse. In that frame the pulse is frozen and the whole string slides backward through it at speed $v$.
The element subtends a small angle $2\theta$ at the centre, so its length is $\Delta\ell = 2R\theta$; tension acts tangentially at each end.
Set the tension force equal to the needed centripetal force. The $\Delta\ell$ and $R$ cancel.
Tighter string is faster; heavier string is slower. No $A$, no $f$ - speed is a property of the string.

segments.text: Time for a board favourite. This derivation shows up as a two or three mark question, and the logic is genuinely elegant, so let us walk it slowly.

The goal is to prove that the speed of a transverse wave on a string is fixed only by two things: the tension you pull it with, and the linear mass density, the mass per unit length. Amplitude and frequency will not appear anywhere.

Here is the clever setup. Take a tiny element of the string right at the crest of the pulse. Because the pulse is curved, that little piece is a short arc of a circle of radius R, subtending a small angle at the centre.

Now the trick that makes everything collapse. Instead of watching the pulse race along, we hop into a frame moving with the pulse. In that frame the pulse is frozen, and the entire string appears to slide backward through it at the wave speed.

Tension pulls on both ends of our element, tangent to the string. The horizontal parts cancel by symmetry; the two inward vertical parts add. Since the angle is small, the sine of the angle is just the angle.
So the net inward force is two T sine theta, which for a small angle becomes two T theta, and using the arc length that tidies up to T times delta ell, over R.

Meanwhile, in our moving frame the element is riding a circular arc at speed v, so it demands a centripetal force pointing to the centre: mass times v squared over R, where the mass is mu times delta ell.

<excited>Here is the whole engine of the proof.</excited> Nothing else is acting, so the tension force must be exactly the centripetal force. We set them equal, and beautifully the little length delta ell and the radius R both cancel.
What survives is T equals mu v squared. Rearrange, and the wave speed is the square root of tension over mass per length.

Read the physics off it. A tighter string carries the wave faster; a heavier string slows it down. And crucially, no amplitude and no frequency anywhere. Speed belongs to the string, not to your hand.
अब एक board favourite। ये derivation two या three mark का question बनता है, और इसकी logic सच में elegant है, तो धीरे-धीरे चलते हैं।

Goal ये prove करना है कि string पर transverse wave की speed सिर्फ़ दो चीज़ों से तय होती है — tension जिससे तुम खींचते हो, और linear mass density यानी mass per unit length। Amplitude और frequency कहीं नहीं आएँगे।
ये देखो clever setup। Pulse के crest पर string का एक tiny element लो। Pulse curved है, तो वो छोटा टुकड़ा radius R वाले circle का एक short arc है, centre पर एक small angle subtend करता।

अब वो trick जो सब कुछ collapse कर देती है। Pulse को दौड़ते देखने के बजाय हम pulse के साथ move करने वाले frame में कूद जाते हैं। उस frame में pulse frozen है, और पूरी string speed v से पीछे की तरफ़ slide करती दिखती है।
Tension element के दोनों ends पर tangent खींचती है। Horizontal parts symmetry से cancel; दोनों inward vertical parts add। Angle small है, तो sine of angle बस angle के बराबर है।
तो net inward force two T sine theta है, जो small angle के लिए two T theta बनती है, और arc length लगाने पर T into delta ell, over R में सिमट जाती है।
उधर moving frame में element circular arc पर speed v से चल रहा है, तो उसे centre की तरफ़ centripetal force चाहिए — mass into v squared over R, जहाँ mass है mu into delta ell।

यही है proof का पूरा engine। और कुछ act कर ही नहीं रहा, तो tension force बिल्कुल centripetal force के बराबर होनी चाहिए। दोनों को equal रखो, और खूबसूरती से delta ell और radius R दोनों cancel हो जाते हैं।
<excited>जो बचता है वो है T equals mu v squared।</excited> Rearrange करो, और wave speed बनती है square root of tension over mass per length।

Physics पढ़ो इससे। Tighter string wave को तेज़ ले जाती है; heavier string उसे धीमा करती है। और सबसे ज़रूरी — कहीं amplitude नहीं, कहीं frequency नहीं। Speed string की property है, तुम्हारे हाथ की नहीं।

sections.title: The wave toolkit: master relations

board_events.text: Your wave toolkit - the master relations
For a wave moving in the minus-$x$ direction, the sign between $\omega t$ and $kx$ flips to plus.

board_events.latex: v_p = \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} = A\omega\cos(\omega t - kx), \quad (v_p)_{\max} = A\omega

board_events.text: Frequency $f$ is set by the source. Crossing into a new medium, $v$ and $\lambda$ change together so $v=f\lambda$ still holds.

segments.text: Let us lay out the complete toolkit for this subtopic. Keep these on speed dial; almost every wave problem is one of them in disguise.

The master relation ties it all together: wave speed equals frequency times wavelength, which also equals wavelength over time period, and equals angular frequency over wave number. Four faces of one truth.
Two bridges to the angular world: angular frequency omega is two pi times frequency, or two pi over the period; and the wave number k is two pi over the wavelength.
The equation of a travelling wave heading in the plus x direction: y equals A sine of omega t minus k x plus a phase constant.
One sign warning. If the wave travels the other way, in the minus x direction, the minus between omega t and k x becomes a plus. That single sign is a favourite trap.
For a transverse wave on a stretched string, the speed is the square root of tension over linear mass density. Notice again, only string properties.

Do not confuse the particle velocity with the wave velocity. A particle of the string moves at A omega cosine of the phase, peaking at A omega. That is how fast a bit of string wiggles, not how fast the pattern travels.

<whisper>A sanity note worth gold in exams.</whisper> The frequency is locked by the source. When a wave crosses into a new medium, the speed and the wavelength both change, but together, so that speed equals frequency times wavelength never breaks.
इस subtopic का पूरा toolkit एक जगह रख लेते हैं। इन्हें speed dial पर रखो; लगभग हर wave problem इन्हीं में से किसी का disguise है।
Master relation सब कुछ जोड़ती है — wave speed बराबर frequency into wavelength, जो wavelength over time period भी है, और angular frequency over wave number भी। एक ही सच के चार चेहरे।
Angular world तक दो पुल — angular frequency omega है two pi into frequency, या two pi over period; और wave number k है two pi over wavelength।
Plus x direction में जाती travelling wave का equation — y बराबर A sine of omega t minus k x plus एक phase constant।
<whisper>एक sign warning।</whisper> अगर wave उल्टी तरफ़, minus x direction में जाए, तो omega t और k x के बीच का minus plus बन जाता है। यही एक sign favourite trap है।
Stretched string पर transverse wave की speed है square root of tension over linear mass density। फिर वही — सिर्फ़ string की properties।
Particle velocity को wave velocity से मत उलझाओ। String का particle A omega cosine of phase से चलता है, peak पर A omega। ये string के टुकड़े की wiggle speed है, pattern की travel speed नहीं।

और exam में सोने जैसा एक sanity note। Frequency source से locked है। Wave नए medium में जाए तो speed और wavelength दोनों बदलते हैं, पर साथ-साथ, ताकि speed equals frequency into wavelength कभी टूटे नहीं।

board_events.text: Given: mass per length $\mu = 0.04$ kg/m, tension $T = 36$ N, frequency $f = 50$ Hz. Find the wave speed and wavelength.
Step 1: get the speed from the string formula - it needs no frequency.
Step 2: now bring in the frequency through $v = f\lambda$.
The string sets the speed; the source frequency then fixes the wavelength.

segments.text: Let us put the string formula to work on a real sitar string. This is exactly the flavour of a two or three mark board question.

Here is the picture. The string is stretched under a tension of thirty-six newtons, it has a mass per unit length of zero point zero four kilograms per metre, and a wave of frequency fifty hertz is set up on it. We want the wave speed and the wavelength.
Reading off the data: mass per length zero point zero four, tension thirty-six, frequency fifty. Two questions, and they come in order.
Step one, the speed. The string formula gives everything we need without touching the frequency.
Speed is the square root of tension over mass per length, that is thirty-six divided by zero point zero four, which is nine hundred, and the square root of nine hundred is thirty metres per second.
Step two, the wavelength. Now, and only now, does the source frequency enter, through the master relation speed equals frequency times wavelength.
Rearranging, wavelength is speed over frequency, thirty over fifty, which is zero point six metres.
Notice the order of operations. The string alone set the speed; then the frequency you chose to play at carved that speed into a wavelength of zero point six metres.
String formula को एक असली sitar string पर लगाते हैं। ये बिल्कुल two या three mark वाले board question का flavour है।

ये रही picture। String thirty-six newton tension पर खिंची है, उसका mass per unit length zero point zero four kilogram per metre है, और उस पर fifty hertz की wave set है। हमें wave speed और wavelength चाहिए।
Data पढ़ लो — mass per length zero point zero four, tension thirty-six, frequency fifty। दो सवाल, और वो order में आते हैं।
Step one, speed। String formula frequency को छुए बिना ही सब दे देता है।
Speed है square root of tension over mass per length, यानी thirty-six divided by zero point zero four, जो nine hundred है, और nine hundred का square root है thirty metre per second।
Step two, wavelength। अब, और अभी ही, source frequency आती है, master relation speed equals frequency into wavelength के ज़रिए।
Rearrange करो — wavelength है speed over frequency, thirty over fifty, यानी zero point six metre।
Order of operations देखो। अकेली string ने speed तय की; फिर जिस frequency पर तुमने बजाया उसने उस speed को zero point six metre की wavelength में काट दिया।

board_events.text: String A has twice the diameter of B and four times the tension. Find $v_A : v_B$.
The trap: seeing four times the tension and blurting 2 : 1, forgetting the thicker string is heavier.
Same material means same density, so $\mu = \rho\cdot\dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} \propto d^2$.
The tension boost is exactly cancelled by the extra mass. Answer: 1 : 1.

segments.text: <curious>Here is a N E E T classic that looks intimidating and quietly equals one. Two strings, A and B, same material. String A has twice the diameter of B and sits under four times the tension. What is the ratio of their wave speeds?
Picture them as in the figure. A is the fat string, pulled hard with four times the tension; B is the thin string under plain tension T. Same material, so the same underlying density.
The question wants the ratio of wave speed on A to wave speed on B.

And here is the trap almost everyone falls into. They see four times the tension, take the square root, and shout two to one, completely forgetting that a thicker string is also heavier per unit length.
Fix that. Same material means the same density, so the linear mass density is density times cross-section area, and area goes as diameter squared. So mu is proportional to diameter squared.
Twice the diameter therefore means four times the mass per length. The ratio of mu A to mu B is two squared, which is four.
Now put it together. The speed ratio is the square root of the tension ratio times the inverse mass ratio, that is the square root of four times one quarter, which is the square root of one.
So the answer is one to one. The extra pull is exactly undone by the extra weight, a textbook looks-complicated-but-equals-one trap. Slow down and it is trivial.

<curious>ये एक N E E T classic है जो डरावना दिखता है और चुपचाप one के बराबर निकलता है। दो strings, A और B, same material। String A का diameter B से double, और tension चार गुना। इनकी wave speeds का ratio क्या है?
Figure की तरह picture करो। A मोटी string है, चार गुना tension से खिंची; B पतली string plain tension T पर। Same material, तो same underlying density।
Question चाहता है A की wave speed और B की wave speed का ratio।
और यहीं वो trap है जिसमें लगभग सब गिरते हैं। चार गुना tension देखा, square root लिया, और two to one चिल्ला दिया, ये भूलकर कि मोटी string per unit length भारी भी है।
इसे ठीक करो। Same material यानी same density, तो linear mass density है density into cross-section area, और area diameter squared की तरह बढ़ता है। तो mu diameter squared के proportional है।
Double diameter का मतलब four times mass per length। mu A to mu B का ratio है two squared, यानी four।
अब जोड़ो। Speed ratio है square root of tension ratio into inverse mass ratio, यानी square root of four into one quarter, जो square root of one है।
तो answer है one to one। Extra खिंचाव को extra वज़न बिल्कुल undo कर देता है। धीरे चलो तो trivial है।

sections.title: Worked example: decode a wave equation

board_events.text: Worked example: decode a wave equation (JEE Main)

board_events.caption: A snapshot of y = 0.05 sin(8 pi t - 4 pi x)

board_events.text: Compare $y = 0.05\sin(8\pi t - 4\pi x)$ with $y = A\sin(\omega t - kx)$.
Max particle speed here is less than the wave speed - they are different quantities.

segments.text: This is the bread and butter of J E E Main waves: hand you an equation, ask you to read its whole life story off it.
The wave is y equals zero point zero five sine of eight pi t minus four pi x, in S I units. The graph shows one snapshot: the height is the amplitude, one full cycle along x is the wavelength.
The whole trick is pattern matching against the standard form y equals A sine of omega t minus k x. Line them up term by term.
The amplitude is read straight off, zero point zero five metres. The coefficient of t is omega, eight pi, so the frequency, omega over two pi, is four hertz.

The coefficient of x is the wave number k, four pi, so the wavelength, two pi over k, is zero point five metres. And the wave speed, omega over k, is eight pi over four pi, a clean two metres per second.
Part b wants the maximum particle speed, which is amplitude times omega, zero point zero five times eight pi, about one point two six metres per second.
Part c: given a mass per length of zero point five, the tension follows from T equals mu v squared, that is zero point five times two squared, two newtons.

<whisper>And do look at part b again.</whisper> The fastest a particle moves, one point two six, is less than the wave speed of two. Particle speed and wave speed are simply different animals; either one can be the larger.
ये J E E Main waves की bread and butter है — तुम्हें equation दे दिया, और उसकी पूरी life story उसी से पढ़वा दी।
Wave है y equals zero point zero five sine of eight pi t minus four pi x, S I units में। Graph एक snapshot दिखाता है — height amplitude है, x के साथ एक पूरा cycle wavelength।
पूरा trick standard form y equals A sine of omega t minus k x से pattern matching का है। Term by term line up करो।
Amplitude सीधे पढ़ लो, zero point zero five metre। t का coefficient omega है, eight pi, तो frequency, omega over two pi, है four hertz।

<excited>x का coefficient wave number k है, four pi, तो wavelength, two pi over k, है zero point five metre, और wave speed, omega over k, है eight pi over four pi, साफ़ two metre per second।</excited>
Part b maximum particle speed चाहता है, जो amplitude into omega है, zero point zero five into eight pi, लगभग one point two six metre per second।
Part c — mass per length zero point five दिया है, तो tension आता है T equals mu v squared से, यानी zero point five into two squared, two newton।
और part b को फिर देखो। Particle की सबसे तेज़ speed, one point two six, wave speed two से कम है। Particle speed और wave speed बिल्कुल अलग जानवर हैं; कोई भी बड़ा हो सकता है।

board_events.text: Rope: $M = 5$ kg, $L = 2$ m, with a block $m = 4$ kg at the bottom. Find the time for a pulse to reach the top ($g = 10$).
Key: tension is NOT constant. Every point supports the weight below it, so $v$ changes with height.
Slowest at the bottom, fastest at the top. Integrate the changing speed - a single average speed is wrong.

segments.text: Now the J E E Advanced version, where the string formula stops being plug and play and becomes real physics.

A uniform rope of mass five kilograms and length two metres hangs from the ceiling, and a four kilogram block dangles from its bottom end. We give the very bottom a flick and ask how long the pulse takes to climb to the top.
The data is on the board, and gravity is ten metres per second squared.

Here is the insight that separates the ones who get it. The tension in the rope is not constant. Every point has to hold up everything hanging below it, so as the pulse climbs, there is more weight beneath it, more tension, and a higher speed. You cannot use one value of v.

First the mass per length: five over two is two point five kilograms per metre. The tension at a height x above the bottom is the block plus the rope below that point, all times g, which is four plus two point five x, times ten.
Divide by mu and take the root, and the local speed becomes two times the square root of four plus two point five x. It genuinely depends on where you are.

Since speed varies, we integrate little time equals little distance over speed, from zero to two. Substitute u equals four plus two point five x, and the integral collapses to one fifth times the bracket two root u from four to nine, giving zero point four seconds.

The physical check seals it. The pulse crawls at the bottom where tension is least and speeds up as it climbs. Anyone who plugs in a single average speed gets the wrong time. Integrating the changing speed is the entire game.
अब J E E Advanced version, जहाँ string formula plug and play से हटकर असली physics बन जाता है।

Five kilogram mass और two metre length वाली uniform rope ceiling से लटकी है, और उसके निचले सिरे से four kilogram का block झूल रहा है। हम एकदम bottom को flick देते हैं और पूछते हैं कि pulse को top तक चढ़ने में कितना time लगता है।
Data board पर है, और gravity ten metre per second squared है।

यहाँ वो insight है जो समझने वालों को अलग करती है। Rope में tension constant नहीं है। हर point को अपने नीचे लटकी हर चीज़ को थामना है, तो pulse जैसे-जैसे चढ़ता है, उसके नीचे ज़्यादा weight, ज़्यादा tension, और ज़्यादा speed। एक ही v काम नहीं करेगी।
पहले mass per length — five over two यानी two point five kilogram per metre। Bottom से height x पर tension है block plus उसके नीचे की rope, सब into g, यानी four plus two point five x, into ten।
mu से divide करके root लो, तो local speed बनती है two into square root of four plus two point five x। ये सच में इस पर depend करती है कि तुम कहाँ हो।

Speed varies करती है, तो हम little time equals little distance over speed को zero से two तक integrate करते हैं। u equals four plus two point five x substitute करो, और integral सिमटकर one fifth into bracket two root u from four to nine बनता है, जो zero point four second देता है।

Physical check इसे seal कर देता है। Pulse bottom पर रेंगता है जहाँ tension सबसे कम, और चढ़ते हुए तेज़ होता है। जो single average speed लगाएगा उसका time गलत आएगा। बदलती speed को integrate करना ही पूरा खेल है।

sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Common pitfalls and pro-tips
Pitfall 1: confusing particle velocity with wave velocity - different formulas, either can be larger.
Wave speed $v = \omega/k$ is how fast the pattern moves; particle speed $v_p = A\omega\cos(\dots)$ is how fast a bit of medium wiggles.
Pitfall 2: forgetting $\mu$ scales with thickness - for same material $\mu \propto d^2 \propto r^2$.
Pitfall 3: assuming frequency changes across media - it does not; $v$ and $\lambda$ do.
Pitfall 4: using one wave speed for a hanging rope - tension varies, so you must integrate.
Pro-tip: for same-material string ratios, use $v \propto \sqrt{T}/r$ and plug ratios straight in.
That single shortcut turns a two-minute problem into ten seconds and dodges the mass-scaling trap automatically.

segments.text: Let us gather the traps that quietly cost marks in this subtopic, then hand you one shortcut that pays for itself.
Trap one, the big one. Do not confuse particle velocity with wave velocity. They are genuinely different quantities with different formulas.

The wave speed, omega over k, is how fast the pattern travels down the string. The particle speed, amplitude times omega cosine of the phase, is how fast one little bit of string bobs. As our J E E example showed, either one can be the larger.

Trap two. In same-material problems, remember the mass per length scales with thickness. A thicker string has a larger mu, going as diameter squared, which is radius squared. Ignoring this is the single most common error in two-string ratios.
Trap three. When a wave enters a new medium, the frequency stays fixed. It is the speed and the wavelength that change. Many students wrongly freeze the wavelength instead.
Trap four. For a vertical hanging rope, the tension varies along its length, so the speed varies too. You must integrate; a constant-speed shortcut gives the wrong time.
Now the reward. For same-material, different-dimension string problems, skip the full grind. Write wave speed as proportional to root T over radius, and plug the ratios straight in.
<whisper>That one move turns a two-minute problem into a ten-second one, and dodges the mass-scaling trap automatically.</whisper> Trust it once and you will never go back.
इस subtopic के वो traps इकट्ठे कर लेते हैं जो चुपचाप marks खाते हैं, फिर एक shortcut देते हैं जो खुद अपनी कीमत वसूल कर देता है।
Trap one, सबसे बड़ा। Particle velocity को wave velocity से मत उलझाओ। ये सच में अलग quantities हैं, अलग formulas के साथ।

Wave speed, omega over k, बताती है pattern string पर कितनी तेज़ चलता है। Particle speed, amplitude into omega cosine of phase, बताती है string का एक टुकड़ा कितनी तेज़ bob करता है। जैसा हमारे J E E example में दिखा, कोई भी बड़ा हो सकता है।

Trap two। Same-material problems में याद रखो mass per length thickness के साथ scale होता है। मोटी string का mu बड़ा, diameter squared यानी radius squared की तरह। इसे ignore करना two-string ratios की सबसे common गलती है।
Trap three। Wave नए medium में जाए तो frequency fixed रहती है। बदलते हैं speed और wavelength। बहुत students गलती से wavelength को freeze कर देते हैं।
Trap four। Vertical hanging rope में tension length के साथ बदलता है, तो speed भी बदलती है। Integrate करना ही पड़ेगा; constant-speed shortcut गलत time देता है।
<excited>अब reward। Same-material, अलग dimension वाली string problems में पूरा grind छोड़ो, wave speed को root T over radius के proportional लिखो, और ratios सीधे plug कर दो।</excited>
वो एक move two-minute problem को ten second में बदल देता है, और mass-scaling trap को अपने आप dodge कर देता है। एक बार trust करो, फिर कभी वापस नहीं जाओगे।

sections.title: The principle of superposition

board_events.text: The principle of superposition

board_events.caption: Waves add point by point, then move on unchanged

board_events.text: When waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of each wave's displacement.
Where two crests meet, the medium rises extra high (constructive). Crest meeting trough nearly cancels (destructive).
Waves do not collide like cricket balls. They add, then pass through each other unchanged.
In phase ($\phi = 0$): amplitudes add, loudest. Out of phase ($\phi = \pi$): they subtract, quietest.

segments.text: <curious>Throw two pebbles into a still pond a little apart. Two sets of ripples spread, meet in the middle, and then, remarkably, keep going as if nothing happened. What actually occurred where they crossed?

The figure holds the whole answer. On the left, two waves arriving in step add up to a bigger wave. On the right, arriving exactly out of step, they flatten each other. In both cases they simply pass through and carry on unchanged.

That is the principle of superposition, the one idea under this whole subtopic. When two or more waves overlap at a point, the resultant displacement there is the algebraic sum of the displacements each wave would have produced alone.
In symbols, y is just y one plus y two plus y three and so on. Plain addition, point by point, instant by instant.
So where two crests coincide, the surface rises extra high, that is constructive. Where a crest lands on a trough, they nearly cancel, that is destructive.
The mental picture to keep is this. Waves do not collide and bounce like cricket balls. They add where they meet, then continue on their way completely unchanged.

For two waves of the same frequency with a phase difference phi, the resultant amplitude is the square root of A one squared plus A two squared plus twice A one A two cosine phi. The cosine term is where all the interference lives.

Read the extremes. In phase, phi zero, the cosine is plus one and the amplitudes fully add, loudest and brightest. Out of phase, phi equals pi, the cosine is minus one and they subtract, quietest and darkest, dead zero if they are equal.

<curious>Still pond में दो pebbles थोड़ी दूरी पर फेंको। Ripples के दो sets फैलते हैं, बीच में मिलते हैं, और फिर हैरानी से ऐसे चलते रहते हैं जैसे कुछ हुआ ही न हो। जहाँ वो cross हुए वहाँ actually क्या हुआ?

Figure में पूरा जवाब है। बाईं तरफ़ दो waves step में आकर एक बड़ी wave बनाती हैं। दाईं तरफ़ बिल्कुल out of step आकर एक-दूसरे को flatten कर देती हैं। दोनों case में वो बस pass through करके unchanged आगे बढ़ जाती हैं।

यही principle of superposition है, इस पूरे subtopic के नीचे की एक idea। जब दो या ज़्यादा waves एक point पर overlap करती हैं, वहाँ resultant displacement उन displacements का algebraic sum है जो हर wave अकेली पैदा करती।
Symbols में, y बस y one plus y two plus y three वग़ैरह है। Plain addition, point by point, instant by instant।
तो जहाँ दो crests मिलते हैं, surface extra ऊँचा उठता है, वो constructive। जहाँ crest किसी trough पर पड़े, वो लगभग cancel, वो destructive।
जो mental picture रखनी है वो ये — waves cricket balls की तरह टकराकर bounce नहीं करतीं। जहाँ मिलती हैं add होती हैं, फिर बिल्कुल unchanged अपने रास्ते चलती रहती हैं।

Same frequency की दो waves के लिए, phase difference phi के साथ, resultant amplitude है square root of A one squared plus A two squared plus twice A one A two cosine phi। सारा interference उस cosine term में बसता है।

<excited>Extremes पढ़ो। In phase, phi zero, cosine plus one और amplitudes पूरे add, सबसे loud। Out of phase, phi equals pi, cosine minus one और वो subtract, सबसे quiet, बराबर हों तो dead zero।</excited>

sections.title: Beats: a note that throbs

board_events.text: Beats - a note that throbs

board_events.caption: Two close frequencies drift in and out of step

board_events.text: Two waves of almost equal frequency drift into phase (loud) and out of phase (soft), over and over.
This periodic rise and fall in loudness is called beats.
The number of loud-soft cycles per second equals the difference of the two frequencies.
A tabla or sitar is tuned by ear this way: adjust tension until the throb slows and vanishes.
Beats need close frequencies. Beyond about 7 Hz the throbs blur together.

segments.text: Now a beautiful cousin of superposition. What happens when the two waves have almost the same frequency, but not quite?

Picture two singers holding the same note in a bhajan, but one is a hair sharp. You do not hear two notes; you hear one note whose loudness swells and fades, over and over. The dashed envelope in the figure is exactly that slow rise and fall.

Here is the mechanism. Because the frequencies differ a little, the two waves slowly drift in and out of step at your ear. For a moment they are in phase and reinforce, loud; then they slip out of phase and cancel, soft; then back in, loud again.
That periodic swelling and fading of loudness is what we call beats. Waaah, waaah, waaah.
<excited>And the count is astonishingly clean. The beat frequency, the number of throbs per second, equals the absolute difference of the two frequencies.</excited>
So two forks close in pitch produce throbs at exactly how far apart they are. Nothing fancier than a subtraction.
This is precisely how a tabla player or a sitarist tunes by ear. They tighten or loosen until the throbbing slows down and finally vanishes. No throb means the two frequencies have matched.
One limit worth knowing. Beats only work when the frequencies are close. Push the gap past about seven hertz and the throbs come too fast for your ear to resolve; you just hear a blur.
<curious>अब superposition का एक ख़ूबसूरत cousin। क्या हो जब दो waves की frequency लगभग same हो, पर बिल्कुल same न हो?

Bhajan में दो singers को same note पकड़े हुए सोचो, पर एक ज़रा sharp है। तुम्हें दो notes नहीं सुनाई देते; एक ही note सुनाई देता है जिसकी loudness बार-बार swell और fade होती है। Figure में dashed envelope बिल्कुल वही slow उतार-चढ़ाव है।

Mechanism ये है। Frequencies थोड़ी अलग हैं, तो दोनों waves तुम्हारे कान पर धीरे-धीरे in और out of step drift करती हैं। एक पल in phase, reinforce, loud; फिर out of phase, cancel, soft; फिर वापस in, loud।
Loudness का वो periodic swell और fade ही beats कहलाता है। वाह, वाह, वाह।
और count हैरान करने वाला साफ़ है। Beat frequency, यानी throbs per second, दोनों frequencies के absolute difference के बराबर है।
तो pitch में पास दो forks उतने ही throbs देते हैं जितने वो दूर हैं। एक subtraction से ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं।
तबला या sitar player बिल्कुल ऐसे ही कान से tune करता है। Tension कसते या ढीला करते हैं जब तक throb धीमा होकर ग़ायब न हो जाए। No throb यानी दोनों frequencies match कर गईं।
एक limit जानने लायक। Beats तभी काम करते हैं जब frequencies पास हों। Gap को लगभग seven hertz से आगे धकेलो तो throbs इतने तेज़ आते हैं कि कान resolve नहीं कर पाता; बस एक blur सुनाई देता है।

sections.title: Board derivation: why beats equal the difference

board_events.text: Board derivation: why beats = the difference
Two equal-amplitude sound waves at close frequencies arrive at one point. Drop the space part; keep time.

board_events.latex: y_1 = A\cos(2\pi f_1 t), \quad y_2 = A\cos(2\pi f_2 t)

board_events.caption: Loudness peaks twice per envelope cycle

board_events.text: Second factor: a fast note at the average frequency. First factor: a slow amplitude envelope.
Loudness depends on the magnitude of the envelope, which peaks twice per cycle - once at plus, once at minus.

segments.text: Let us actually derive the beat formula, because the factor of two at the end is exactly what students drop, and this shows where it comes from.

Set up. Two sound waves of equal amplitude and slightly different frequencies reach one fixed point, say your eardrum. Since beats are about how loudness changes in time at one place, we keep only the time dependence and drop the spatial part.
Write the two arrivals as cosines: y one is A cosine of two pi f one t, and y two is A cosine of two pi f two t.

Add them by superposition and use the sum-to-product identity for cosine plus cosine. The sum becomes two A, times cosine of two pi times half the difference frequency t, times cosine of two pi times the average frequency t.
Now read the two timescales off the figure. There are two very different rhythms living in one expression.

The second factor is a fast oscillation at the average of the two frequencies, that is the actual note your ear perceives. The first factor changes lazily, because half the difference is tiny; that is the slow amplitude envelope, the swelling and fading.

<whisper>And here is the crucial step almost everyone misses.</whisper> Loudness depends on the magnitude of that envelope, not its sign. The envelope reaches maximum loudness twice in each of its own cycles, once when the cosine is plus one, once when it is minus one.

So the loudness throbs at twice the envelope frequency. Two times half the difference is simply the full difference. That factor of two is the whole reason the answer is the clean difference, not half of it.
अब beat formula सच में derive करते हैं, क्योंकि आख़िर में जो factor of two है वही students drop कर देते हैं, और ये दिखाता है वो आता कहाँ से है।

Set up। Equal amplitude और थोड़ी अलग frequencies वाली दो sound waves एक fixed point पर पहुँचती हैं, मान लो तुम्हारा कान का पर्दा। Beats एक जगह पर loudness के time के साथ बदलने के बारे में हैं, तो हम सिर्फ़ time dependence रखते हैं और spatial part छोड़ देते हैं।
दोनों arrivals को cosines में लिखो — y one है A cosine of two pi f one t, और y two है A cosine of two pi f two t।

Superposition से add करो और cosine plus cosine वाली sum-to-product identity लगाओ। Sum बन जाता है two A, into cosine of two pi into half the difference frequency t, into cosine of two pi into average frequency t।
अब figure से दो timescales पढ़ो। एक ही expression में दो बहुत अलग rhythms रहते हैं।

दूसरा factor average frequency पर एक fast oscillation है, वही note जो तुम्हारा कान perceive करता है। पहला factor आलस से बदलता है, क्योंकि half the difference बहुत छोटी है; वही slow amplitude envelope है, swell और fade।

और यहाँ वो crucial step जो लगभग सब miss करते हैं। Loudness उस envelope की magnitude पर depend करती है, sign पर नहीं। Envelope अपने हर cycle में दो बार maximum loudness छूता है, एक बार जब cosine plus one, एक बार जब minus one।

<excited>तो loudness envelope frequency से दोगुनी दर पर throb करती है। Two into half the difference बस full difference है। वही factor of two पूरी वजह है कि answer साफ़ difference है, आधा नहीं।</excited>

sections.title: Superposition and beats: the toolkit

board_events.text: Superposition and beats - the toolkit
Constructive: path difference $\Delta x = n\lambda$. Destructive: $\Delta x = (2n+1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$.
Loading a fork with wax lowers its frequency; filing it raises the frequency.

segments.text: The consolidated toolkit for superposition and beats. This is your complete reference for the whole subtopic.
First, superposition itself. The resultant displacement is just the sum of the individual displacements, y one plus y two and onward.
For two same-frequency waves with phase difference phi, the resultant amplitude is the square root of A one squared plus A two squared plus twice A one A two cosine phi.
Since intensity goes as amplitude squared, the resultant intensity is I one plus I two plus twice the root of I one I two, all times cosine phi. That last term is the interference.
The extremes: maximum intensity is the square of root I one plus root I two; minimum intensity is the square of their difference. These give you the bright and dark fringes.
For the conditions in terms of path difference: constructive interference needs a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths; destructive needs an odd number of half wavelengths.
The beat frequency is the absolute difference of the two frequencies, and phase difference relates to path difference by two pi over lambda times delta x.
And the tuning-fork rule you must memorise. Loading a fork with wax lowers its frequency; filing a fork raises it. Master one and the other follows.
Superposition और beats का consolidated toolkit। ये पूरे subtopic के लिए तुम्हारा complete reference है।
पहले superposition खुद। Resultant displacement बस individual displacements का sum है, y one plus y two और आगे।
Same-frequency की दो waves के लिए, phase difference phi के साथ, resultant amplitude है square root of A one squared plus A two squared plus twice A one A two cosine phi।
Intensity amplitude squared की तरह चलती है, तो resultant intensity है I one plus I two plus twice root of I one I two, into cosine phi। वो last term ही interference है।
Extremes — maximum intensity है root I one plus root I two का square; minimum intensity उनके difference का square। यही तुम्हें bright और dark fringes देते हैं।
Path difference वाली conditions — constructive interference के लिए path difference whole number of wavelengths चाहिए; destructive के लिए odd number of half wavelengths।
Beat frequency दोनों frequencies का absolute difference है, और phase difference, path difference से two pi over lambda into delta x के ज़रिए जुड़ती है।
और tuning-fork rule जो रटना ज़रूरी है। Fork पर wax load करने से उसकी frequency गिरती है; fork को file करने से frequency बढ़ती है। एक याद कर लो, दूसरा अपने आप आ जाता है।

sections.title: Worked example: two tuning forks

board_events.text: Worked example: two tuning forks (CBSE level)
Forks of 512 Hz and 516 Hz are sounded together. Find the beat frequency and the time between loudness maxima.
So you hear four swells of loudness every second - the forks are four hertz apart.
The time between successive loud moments is just the beat period.
Beat period is the reciprocal of beat frequency: a bigger gap means faster throbs.
Answer: 4 beats per second, with maxima 0.25 s apart.

segments.text: A clean board-level warm up before the traps. Two tuning forks, one at five hundred twelve hertz, one at five hundred sixteen hertz, are sounded together.
We want two things: the beat frequency, and the time gap between two successive maxima of loudness.
The beat frequency is just the absolute difference, five hundred sixteen minus five hundred twelve, which is four hertz.
So you hear four swells of loudness every second. The forks are four hertz apart, and that is literally the throb rate.
For part b, the time between successive loud moments is simply the beat period, the reciprocal of the beat frequency.
One over four is zero point two five seconds between maxima.
Keep the relationship in your bones. Beat period is one over beat frequency, so a bigger frequency gap means faster, more frequent throbs.
Final answer, four beats per second, with the loud moments spaced a quarter of a second apart.
Traps से पहले एक साफ़ board-level warm up। दो tuning forks, एक five hundred twelve hertz पर, एक five hundred sixteen hertz पर, साथ बजाई जाती हैं।
दो चीज़ें चाहिए — beat frequency, और loudness के दो successive maxima के बीच का time gap।
Beat frequency बस absolute difference है, five hundred sixteen minus five hundred twelve, यानी four hertz।
तो तुम हर second loudness के four swells सुनते हो। Forks four hertz दूर हैं, और वही throb rate है।
Part b के लिए, दो loud पलों के बीच का time बस beat period है, beat frequency का reciprocal।
One over four यानी zero point two five second maxima के बीच।
Relationship हड्डियों में बिठा लो। Beat period है one over beat frequency, तो बड़ा frequency gap यानी तेज़, ज़्यादा बार throbs।
Final answer — four beats per second, loud पल एक quarter second की दूरी पर।

board_events.text: Fork A gives 6 beats/s with a 480 Hz standard. Loading A with wax drops the beat to 3/s. Find A's original frequency.
The trap: stopping at 486 or 474 and guessing. Use the loading clue to choose.
Rule: wax lowers a fork's frequency, so loading A pushes it downward.
If A were 486, loading moves it toward 480, beats fall to 3 (matches). If A were 474, loading moves it away, beats rise (fails).
Answer: 486 Hz. Beats fell after loading, so the fork was above the standard.

segments.text: <curious>Now a N E E T favourite that punishes guessing. Fork A has an unknown frequency. Sounded with a standard four hundred eighty hertz fork, it gives six beats per second. When you load A with a little wax, the beats drop to three per second. What was A's original frequency?
The number line makes the logic visible. Six beats means A is six hertz from the standard, so it sits at either four hundred eighty-six or four hundred seventy-four.
That is the whole setup. Two candidates, and a clue hiding in the wax.
Here is the trap. Most students stop at four hundred eighty-six or four hundred seventy-four and then simply guess. You must use the loading information to decide, and it fully decides.
So list them honestly. A is four hundred eighty plus or minus six, that is four hundred eighty-six hertz or four hundred seventy-four hertz.
Now the rule. Wax always lowers a fork's frequency, so loading A with wax pushes A downward on that number line.

Test each. If A started at four hundred eighty-six, loading drops it toward four hundred eighty, the two get closer, and the beats fall, which matches the drop to three. If A were four hundred seventy-four, loading drops it away from four hundred eighty, they get farther, and the beats would rise, which fails.
So the answer is four hundred eighty-six hertz. The shortcut to remember: wax lowers; if the beats fell after loading, the fork was above the standard, so pick the higher candidate.

<curious>अब एक N E E T favourite जो guessing को सज़ा देता है। Fork A की frequency unknown है। एक standard four hundred eighty hertz fork के साथ बजाने पर six beats per second देता है। जब A पर थोड़ा wax load करते हो, beats गिरकर three per second हो जाते हैं। A की original frequency क्या थी?
Number line logic को साफ़ दिखाता है। Six beats यानी A standard से six hertz दूर, तो वो या तो four hundred eighty-six पर है या four hundred seventy-four पर।
यही पूरा setup है। दो candidates, और wax में छिपा एक clue।
यहाँ trap है। ज़्यादातर students four hundred eighty-six या four hundred seventy-four पर रुककर बस guess कर लेते हैं। तुम्हें loading वाली जानकारी से decide करना है, और वो पूरी तरह decide कर देती है।
तो ईमानदारी से list करो। A है four hundred eighty plus या minus six, यानी four hundred eighty-six hertz या four hundred seventy-four hertz।
अब rule। Wax हमेशा fork की frequency गिराता है, तो A पर wax load करना A को उस number line पर नीचे धकेलता है।

हर एक test करो। अगर A four hundred eighty-six से शुरू हुआ, loading उसे four hundred eighty की तरफ़ गिराता है, दोनों पास आते हैं, beats गिरते हैं, जो three तक गिरने से match करता है। अगर A four hundred seventy-four होता, loading उसे four hundred eighty से दूर गिराता, वो और दूर होते, beats बढ़ते, जो fail करता है।
<excited>तो answer है four hundred eighty-six hertz। याद रखने का shortcut — wax lowers; अगर loading के बाद beats गिरे, तो fork standard से ऊपर था, तो higher candidate चुनो।</excited>

board_events.text: Two coherent sources give intensities $I$ and $4I$. Find $I_{\max}/I_{\min}$, and the intensity where the phase difference is $\pi/2$.
Amplitudes go as the root of intensity, so $A_1 : A_2 = 1 : 2$.
At $\phi = \pi/2$ the cosine is zero, so the intensities simply add to $5I$.

segments.text: A staple J E E Main interference numerical. Two coherent sources deliver intensities I and four I at a point. Part a asks the ratio of maximum to minimum intensity; part b asks the intensity where the phase difference is pi over two.
Start with the amplitudes, shown in the bars. Amplitude goes as the square root of intensity, so the ratio of amplitudes is one to two, even though the intensities are one to four.
So we have the two ingredients: intensities one and four I, amplitudes in the ratio one to two. Everything else is plugging in.
Set up the extremes using amplitudes. The bright fringe adds them, the dark fringe subtracts them.
Maximum intensity is root I plus root four I, all squared, that is three root I squared, which is nine I. Minimum intensity is two root I minus root I squared, which is just I.
So the contrast ratio, maximum over minimum, is nine to one. That is the visibility of the pattern.
For part b, use the intensity formula with cosine of pi over two, which is zero. The interference term vanishes, and the intensity is simply I plus four I, which is five I.
<whisper>So at a ninety degree phase difference the cross term switches off and you just add the two intensities to five I.</whisper> A common trap if you forget the cosine is zero there.

एक staple J E E Main interference numerical। दो coherent sources एक point पर intensities I और four I देते हैं। Part a maximum to minimum intensity का ratio पूछता है; part b वो intensity जहाँ phase difference pi over two है।
Amplitudes से शुरू करो, bars में दिखी हुई। Amplitude intensity के square root की तरह चलती है, तो amplitudes का ratio one to two है, भले ही intensities one to four हों।
तो दो ingredients मिल गए — intensities one और four I, amplitudes ratio one to two में। बाक़ी सब plugging in है।
Amplitudes से extremes set करो। Bright fringe उन्हें add करता है, dark fringe subtract।
Maximum intensity है root I plus root four I, whole squared, यानी three root I squared, जो nine I है। Minimum intensity है two root I minus root I squared, जो बस I है।
<excited>तो contrast ratio, maximum over minimum, है nine to one। यही pattern की visibility है।</excited>
Part b के लिए, intensity formula में cosine of pi over two लगाओ, जो zero है। Interference term ग़ायब, और intensity बस I plus four I, यानी five I।
तो ninety degree phase difference पर cross term बंद हो जाता है और तुम बस दोनों intensities को five I में add करते हो। Common trap अगर भूल जाओ कि वहाँ cosine zero है।

sections.title: Worked example: a one-newton tension nudge

board_events.text: Worked example: a 1 N tension nudge (JEE Advanced)
Two identical wires at 100 N tension vibrate in unison at 400 Hz. One wire's tension is raised by 1 N. How many beats per second?
Both start at the same frequency, zero beats. The tiny mismatch after the nudge makes beats.
A 1 percent tension rise gives only a 0.5 percent frequency rise - the square root halves it.

segments.text: A lovely J E E Advanced application of small changes. Two identical sonometer wires, each stretched by one hundred newtons, vibrate in perfect unison at four hundred hertz. Now raise the tension in just one wire by one newton. How many beats per second do you hear?

The picture first. Both wires begin at exactly the same frequency, so at the start there are zero beats. Nudging one wire's tension up shifts its frequency a hair, and that tiny mismatch is what produces the beats.
So the real question is: how much does a one newton nudge shift the frequency?
Start from the fundamental, f equals one over two L times root T over mu. Everything except the tension is fixed, so frequency is proportional to the square root of the tension.
For a small change, take logarithms and differentiate. The fractional change in frequency is one half the fractional change in tension. The square root becomes a factor of one half.

Plug in. The change in tension is one newton, the tension is one hundred, the frequency is four hundred, so the change in frequency is one half times one over one hundred times four hundred, which is two hertz.
The stretched wire is now at four hundred two hertz, the other still at four hundred. The beat frequency is their difference, two per second.

The sanity check is elegant. A one percent rise in tension gives only a half percent rise in frequency, because the square root halves it. That is exactly why a tiny tension change gives a small, audible beat rather than a wild jump in pitch.

Small changes का एक प्यारा J E E Advanced application। दो identical sonometer wires, हर एक one hundred newton से खिंची, four hundred hertz पर perfect unison में vibrate करती हैं। अब सिर्फ़ एक wire की tension one newton बढ़ाओ। कितने beats per second सुनाई देते हैं?

पहले picture। दोनों wires बिल्कुल same frequency पर शुरू होती हैं, तो शुरू में zero beats। एक wire की tension ऊपर nudge करने से उसकी frequency ज़रा shift होती है, और वही tiny mismatch beats पैदा करता है।
तो असली सवाल — one newton का nudge frequency को कितना shift करता है?
Fundamental से शुरू करो, f equals one over two L into root T over mu। Tension के अलावा सब fixed है, तो frequency tension के square root के proportional है।
Small change के लिए, logarithms लेकर differentiate करो। Frequency का fractional change tension के fractional change का one half है। Square root एक factor of one half बन जाता है।
Plug in करो। Tension का change one newton, tension one hundred, frequency four hundred, तो frequency का change है one half into one over one hundred into four hundred, यानी two hertz।
खिंची हुई wire अब four hundred two hertz पर है, दूसरी अब भी four hundred पर। Beat frequency उनका difference है, two per second।

Sanity check elegant है। Tension में one percent बढ़ोतरी frequency में सिर्फ़ half percent देती है, क्योंकि square root उसे आधा कर देता है। इसीलिए ज़रा सी tension change एक छोटा, audible beat देती है, pitch में जंगली jump नहीं।

sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Common pitfalls and pro-tips
Pitfall 1: halving the beat frequency. It is $|f_1 - f_2|$, not half. The half belongs to the envelope.
Pitfall 2: mixing loading and filing. Wax lowers frequency; filing raises it.
Pitfall 3: adding intensities for coherent waves. You cannot drop the $2\sqrt{I_1 I_2}\cos\phi$ term.
Only incoherent sources let intensities simply add. Coherent sources carry the interference term.
Pitfall 4: confusing beats with interference. Same frequency gives a spatial pattern; close frequencies give beats in time.
Pro-tip: for loading and filing, just ask whether the fork moved toward or away from the standard, and match the beat change.
That single question replaces all the case-by-case reasoning about plus and minus.

segments.text: Four traps to seal this subtopic, then one clean question that dissolves the loading and filing headache for good.

Trap one, the classic. The beat frequency is the full difference of the two frequencies, not half of it. The one half belongs to the amplitude envelope; the loudness throbs at twice that, so the difference is what you hear.

Trap two. Do not mix up loading and filing. Wax lowers a fork's frequency; filing raises it. Learn one firmly and the other follows, because getting this backward flips your entire plus or minus decision.
Trap three. For coherent sources you cannot simply add intensities. The interference term, twice the root of I one I two times cosine phi, genuinely matters and must be kept.
Only for incoherent sources do intensities just add. The moment the sources are coherent, that cross term is part of the answer.

Trap four. Keep beats and interference apart. Two sources of the same frequency give a steady pattern in space; two nearly equal frequencies give beats, a throb in time. Different phenomena, different formulas.

And the pro-tip that saves you every time. For loading and filing problems, skip the case work and just ask: did the fork move toward the standard or away from it? Then match that to whether the beats went down or up.
That one question replaces all the fiddly plus and minus reasoning. Trust it, and these problems become ten second confirmations.
इस subtopic को seal करने के लिए चार traps, फिर एक साफ़ सवाल जो loading और filing का सिरदर्द हमेशा के लिए घोल देता है।

Trap one, classic। Beat frequency दोनों frequencies का full difference है, आधा नहीं। वो one half amplitude envelope का है; loudness उससे दोगुनी दर पर throb करती है, तो जो तुम सुनते हो वो difference है।

Trap two। Loading और filing को मत उलझाओ। Wax fork की frequency गिराता है; filing बढ़ाता है। एक को मज़बूती से सीखो, दूसरा अपने आप आएगा, क्योंकि इसे उल्टा करना तुम्हारा पूरा plus या minus decision पलट देता है।
Trap three। Coherent sources के लिए तुम बस intensities add नहीं कर सकते। Interference term, twice root of I one I two into cosine phi, सच में मायने रखता है और रखना ही पड़ता है।
सिर्फ़ incoherent sources के लिए intensities बस add होती हैं। जैसे ही sources coherent हुए, वो cross term answer का हिस्सा है।
Trap four। Beats और interference को अलग रखो। Same frequency के दो sources space में एक steady pattern देते हैं; लगभग बराबर दो frequencies beats देती हैं, time में throb। अलग phenomena, अलग formulas।
और वो pro-tip जो हर बार बचाती है। Loading और filing problems में case work छोड़ो और बस पूछो — fork standard की तरफ़ गया या दूर? फिर उसे match करो कि beats गिरे या बढ़े।
<excited>वो एक सवाल सारी fiddly plus और minus reasoning की जगह ले लेता है। Trust करो, और ये problems ten second confirmations बन जाती हैं।</excited>

sections.title: Standing waves: a pattern that goes nowhere

board_events.text: Standing waves - the pattern that stands still

board_events.caption: Nodes stay still; antinodes swing hardest

board_events.text: Pluck a string: a wave travels to the fixed end, reflects, and returns. Two identical waves now move in opposite directions.
They superpose. Points that always cancel are nodes; points that always reinforce are antinodes.
Standing wave = forward wave + its own reflection.
Like a skipping rope two children twirl: the loops just sit between their hands; no energy streams off the ends.
Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart; a node and its neighbouring antinode are a quarter wavelength apart.
Energy is trapped between the boundaries - it sloshes back and forth rather than travelling away.

segments.text: <curious>Pluck a sitar string and watch closely. It does not send a wave racing off to one side. Instead the whole string shimmers in place, some points swinging wildly, others sitting perfectly still. Where did that come from?
The figure captures it. The still points, marked N, are nodes; the points of biggest swing, marked A, are antinodes. The pattern just stands there, going nowhere.
Here is the mechanism. When you pluck the string, a wave travels to the fixed end, reflects, and travels back. Now you have two identical waves moving in opposite directions along the same string.
They superpose. At certain points the two waves always cancel; those dead still points are the nodes. Halfway between, they always reinforce and swing with maximum amplitude; those are the antinodes.
So the one line to remember is this. A standing wave is simply a forward wave plus its own reflection.
Picture a skipping rope two children are twirling. The rope clearly oscillates, but the pattern, one big loop or two or three, just sits between their hands. No energy streams off the ends.

Read the spacing off the figure. Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, and a node and its neighbouring antinode are a quarter wavelength apart. Sketching one loop and labelling it prevents half the errors in this topic.
And that is the deep difference from a travelling wave. Here the energy is trapped between the boundaries. It sloshes back and forth rather than streaming away.
<curious>Sitar की string pluck करके ध्यान से देखो। वो एक तरफ़ wave दौड़ाकर नहीं भेजती। बल्कि पूरी string अपनी जगह shimmer करती है, कुछ points ज़ोर से झूलते, कुछ बिल्कुल स्थिर। ये आया कहाँ से?
Figure इसे पकड़ लेता है। स्थिर points, N से marked, nodes हैं; सबसे बड़े swing वाले points, A से marked, antinodes हैं। Pattern बस वहीं खड़ा रहता है, कहीं नहीं जाता।
Mechanism ये है। जब तुम string pluck करते हो, एक wave fixed end तक जाती है, reflect होती है, और वापस आती है। अब उसी string पर दो identical waves opposite directions में चल रही हैं।
वो superpose करती हैं। कुछ points पर दोनों waves हमेशा cancel करती हैं; वो dead still points nodes हैं। बीच में वो हमेशा reinforce करती हैं और maximum amplitude से झूलती हैं; वो antinodes हैं।
<excited>तो याद रखने वाली एक line — standing wave बस एक forward wave plus उसकी अपनी reflection है।</excited>
दो बच्चों की twirl करती skipping rope सोचो। Rope साफ़ oscillate करती है, पर pattern, एक बड़ा loop या दो या तीन, बस उनके हाथों के बीच बैठा रहता है। Ends से कोई energy नहीं बहती।
Figure से spacing पढ़ो। Adjacent nodes half a wavelength दूर हैं, और node और उसका पड़ोसी antinode a quarter wavelength दूर। एक loop बनाकर label कर लेना इस topic की आधी गलतियाँ रोक देता है।
और यही travelling wave से गहरा फ़र्क़ है। यहाँ energy boundaries के बीच trapped है। वो streaming away के बजाय आगे-पीछे slosh करती है।

sections.title: Harmonics, resonance, and pipes

board_events.text: Bounded media, harmonics, and pipes

board_events.caption: Open pipe: all harmonics; closed pipe: odd only

board_events.text: A bounded medium supports only wavelengths that fit its boundaries. A string fixed at both ends needs a node at each end.
The allowed frequencies are the harmonics; the lowest is the fundamental. Shorter length means higher pitch.
Resonance: drive an air column at a natural frequency and the sound swells - like pushing a swing in rhythm.
Closed end = displacement node (air cannot move). Open end = displacement antinode (air moves freely).
Open pipe (open both ends): antinodes at both ends, supports all harmonics f, 2f, 3f.
Closed pipe (one end closed): node at closed end, antinode at open end - only odd harmonics f, 3f, 5f.

segments.text: Now the idea that turns strings and pipes into musical instruments. A bounded medium is picky about which waves it will hold.
The figure shows the two workhorses of acoustics, an open pipe and a closed pipe, and already hints at why they sound so different.

The rule is this. A bounded medium can only support standing waves whose pattern fits neatly between its boundaries. A string clamped at both ends must have a node at each end, so only certain wavelengths survive; everything else dies out.

Those special allowed frequencies are the harmonics, and the lowest one is the fundamental, or first harmonic. Fewer centimetres means shorter allowed wavelengths, which means higher pitch, which is exactly why a bansuri player raises the pitch by uncovering holes and shortening the air column.

Resonance is the partner idea. Drive an air column at exactly one of its natural frequencies and the sound suddenly swells, because energy pours in efficiently. It is the same physics as pushing a child on a swing at its natural rhythm.
For pipes the boundary rule is about how the air can move. A closed, sealed end forces the air to be still, a displacement node. An open end lets the air move freely, a displacement antinode.
That single rule builds two instruments. An open pipe, open at both ends, has antinodes at both ends and supports every harmonic, f, two f, three f, and so on.

A closed pipe is the interesting one. With a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, it supports only the odd harmonics, f, three f, five f, and its fundamental sits a whole octave below an open pipe of the same length.
अब वो idea जो strings और pipes को musical instruments बना देती है। Bounded medium इस बारे में picky है कि वो कौन सी waves रखेगा।
Figure acoustics के दो workhorses दिखाता है, एक open pipe और एक closed pipe, और अभी से इशारा देता है कि वो इतने अलग क्यों sound करते हैं।

Rule ये है। Bounded medium सिर्फ़ वही standing waves रख सकता है जिनका pattern उसकी boundaries के बीच ठीक बैठे। दोनों सिरों पर clamped string को हर सिरे पर node चाहिए, तो सिर्फ़ कुछ wavelengths बचती हैं; बाक़ी सब मर जाती हैं।

<excited>वो special allowed frequencies harmonics हैं, और सबसे नीची fundamental या first harmonic। कम centimetres यानी छोटी allowed wavelengths, यानी ऊँची pitch, इसीलिए बांसुरी वाला holes खोलकर air column छोटा करके pitch बढ़ाता है।</excited>

Resonance partner idea है। किसी air column को उसकी natural frequency पर drive करो और sound अचानक swell कर जाता है, क्योंकि energy efficiently अंदर बहती है। ये वही physics है जैसे बच्चे को swing पर उसकी natural rhythm में धक्का देना।

Pipes के लिए boundary rule इस बारे में है कि air कैसे move कर सकती है। बंद, sealed end air को स्थिर रहने पर मजबूर करता है, एक displacement node। Open end air को freely move करने देता है, एक displacement antinode।
वो एक rule दो instruments बनाता है। Open pipe, दोनों सिरों पर खुला, दोनों ends पर antinodes रखता है और हर harmonic support करता है, f, two f, three f, वग़ैरह।

Closed pipe दिलचस्प वाला है। Closed end पर node और open end पर antinode के साथ, ये सिर्फ़ odd harmonics support करता है, f, three f, five f, और इसका fundamental same length के open pipe से पूरे एक octave नीचे बैठता है।

sections.title: Board derivation: standing wave and string harmonics

board_events.text: Board derivation: standing wave and string harmonics
Superpose a wave and its reflection: $y_1 = a\sin(kx - \omega t)$, $y_2 = a\sin(kx + \omega t)$.
Space and time have separated: every point oscillates as $\cos(\omega t)$ with a fixed amplitude $2a\sin(kx)$.

board_events.caption: Only whole numbers of half-loops fit length L

board_events.text: A string fixed at both ends needs a node at each end, so $\sin(kL)=0 \Rightarrow L = \tfrac{n\lambda}{2}$.

segments.text: This board derivation comes in two halves: first build the standing wave, then find the harmonics. Both are three to five mark favourites.

Take a wave travelling in the plus x direction and its reflection travelling in the minus x direction, each of amplitude a. A wave hitting a fixed boundary bounces back, so the original and its reflection are exactly what superpose.
Add them by superposition and use the sine plus sine identity. The sum collapses to two a, times sine k x, times cosine omega t.

Now read the physics. Unlike a travelling wave, where x and t are locked together inside one sine, here space and time have separated. Every point oscillates in time as cosine omega t, but its amplitude, two a sine k x, is fixed by where it sits. The pattern does not travel; it stands.

Set the amplitude to zero for nodes: sine k x equals zero gives x at whole multiples of half a wavelength. Set it to maximum for antinodes: those fall at odd multiples of a quarter wavelength. Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, exactly as we saw.
Now the second half, the harmonics, and the figure shows the whole secret. Only a whole number of half loops can fit into the length.

A string clamped at both ends must have a node at each end. The end at zero is already a node; for the far end to be a node too, sine of k L must be zero, which forces L to equal a whole number of half wavelengths.

<excited>So the allowed frequencies are n v over two L, for n one, two, three, and onward. The fundamental is v over two L, and substituting the string speed gives the sonometer master formula, one over two L times root T over mu.</excited>
ये board derivation दो हिस्सों में आती है — पहले standing wave बनाओ, फिर harmonics निकालो। दोनों three से five mark के favourites हैं।

Plus x direction में जाती wave और minus x direction में जाती उसकी reflection लो, हर एक amplitude a की। Fixed boundary से टकराती wave वापस bounce होती है, तो original और उसकी reflection ही superpose करती हैं।
Superposition से add करो और sine plus sine identity लगाओ। Sum सिमटकर two a, into sine k x, into cosine omega t बन जाता है।

<whisper>अब physics पढ़ो। Travelling wave के उलट, जहाँ x और t एक ही sine में locked होते हैं, यहाँ space और time अलग हो गए हैं। हर point time में cosine omega t की तरह oscillate करता है, पर उसका amplitude, two a sine k x, इस बात से fixed है कि वो कहाँ बैठा है। Pattern travel नहीं करता; खड़ा रहता है।</whisper>

Nodes के लिए amplitude zero रखो — sine k x equals zero देता है x whole multiples of half a wavelength पर। Antinodes के लिए maximum रखो — वो odd multiples of a quarter wavelength पर आते हैं। Adjacent nodes half a wavelength दूर, बिल्कुल जैसा हमने देखा।
अब दूसरा हिस्सा, harmonics, और figure पूरा राज़ दिखाता है। सिर्फ़ whole number of half loops ही length में fit होते हैं।

दोनों सिरों पर clamped string को हर सिरे पर node चाहिए। Zero वाला end पहले से node है; दूर वाले end के भी node होने के लिए sine of k L zero होना चाहिए, जो L को whole number of half wavelengths के बराबर कर देता है।

तो allowed frequencies हैं n v over two L, n one, two, three वग़ैरह के लिए। Fundamental है v over two L, और string speed substitute करने पर sonometer master formula मिलता है, one over two L into root T over mu।

sections.title: Standing waves and acoustics: the toolkit

board_events.text: Standing waves and acoustics - the toolkit
Overtones: string/open pipe 1st overtone = 2nd harmonic; closed pipe 1st overtone = 3rd harmonic.

segments.text: The complete reference for standing waves and acoustics. Lock these in; the whole subtopic is built on them.
The standing wave itself: y equals two a sine k x cosine omega t. The amplitude depends on position; that position dependence is the signature of a standing wave.
The spacing you will use constantly: node to node is half a wavelength, and node to nearest antinode is a quarter wavelength.
For a string fixed at both ends, or an open pipe, the frequencies are n v over two L, and it supports every harmonic, all integers n.
For a closed pipe the frequencies are two n minus one, times v over four L, which means only the odd harmonics survive. That single difference drives most pipe problems.

A refinement for precise work: the antinode actually bulges just beyond the open end, so the effective length is the real length plus an end correction of about zero point six times the radius, per open end.

For the resonance tube, two successive resonances at lengths l one and l two give the wavelength as twice their difference, the speed as two f times their difference, and the end correction as l two minus three l one, over two.
And the overtone map you must not fumble. For a string or open pipe, the first overtone is the second harmonic. For a closed pipe, the first overtone leapfrogs to the third harmonic.
Standing waves और acoustics का complete reference। इन्हें lock कर लो; पूरा subtopic इन्हीं पर बना है।
Standing wave खुद — y equals two a sine k x cosine omega t। Amplitude position पर depend करता है; वही position dependence standing wave की पहचान है।
जो spacing तुम बार-बार use करोगे — node to node half a wavelength, और node to nearest antinode a quarter wavelength।
दोनों सिरों पर fixed string, या open pipe, के लिए frequencies हैं n v over two L, और ये हर harmonic support करता है, सारे integers n।
Closed pipe के लिए frequencies हैं two n minus one, into v over four L, यानी सिर्फ़ odd harmonics बचते हैं। वही एक फ़र्क़ ज़्यादातर pipe problems चलाता है।
Precise work के लिए एक refinement — antinode असल में open end से ज़रा आगे उभरता है, तो effective length है real length plus एक end correction लगभग zero point six into radius, हर open end पर।

Resonance tube के लिए, lengths l one और l two पर दो successive resonances wavelength को उनके difference का दोगुना देते हैं, speed को two f into difference, और end correction को l two minus three l one, over two।
और overtone map जो fumble नहीं करना। String या open pipe के लिए first overtone second harmonic है। Closed pipe के लिए first overtone leapfrog करके third harmonic पर जाता है।

sections.title: Worked example: a stretched wire

board_events.text: Worked example: a stretched wire (CBSE level)

board_events.caption: Fundamental and first two overtones

board_events.text: Wire length 0.5 m fixed at both ends, wave speed 200 m/s. Find the fundamental and the first two overtones.
A string supports all harmonics, so the overtones are the higher integer multiples.
First overtone = 2nd harmonic, second overtone = 3rd harmonic (a string skips nothing).
Answer: fundamental 200 Hz; first two overtones 400 Hz and 600 Hz.

segments.text: A clean board warm up on harmonics. A stretched wire zero point five metres long is fixed at both ends, and a transverse wave travels on it at two hundred metres per second. Find the fundamental and its first two overtones.
The figure shows the three modes: one loop, two loops, three loops. Since the wire is fixed at both ends, it hosts every harmonic in that ladder.
The data is short: length zero point five metres, speed two hundred. That is all we need.
The fundamental is v over two L, that is two hundred over two times zero point five, which is two hundred over one, a clean two hundred hertz.
Because a string supports all harmonics, the overtones are simply the next integer multiples of the fundamental. Nothing is skipped.
So the first overtone is twice the fundamental, four hundred hertz, and the second overtone is three times it, six hundred hertz.
Nail the vocabulary here. For a string, the first overtone is the second harmonic and the second overtone is the third harmonic. String and open pipe skip nothing.
Final answer: fundamental two hundred hertz, and the first two overtones four hundred and six hundred hertz.

Harmonics पर एक साफ़ board warm up। zero point five metre लंबी stretched wire दोनों सिरों पर fixed है, और उस पर transverse wave two hundred metre per second से चलती है। Fundamental और उसके first two overtones निकालो।
Figure तीन modes दिखाता है — one loop, two loops, three loops। Wire दोनों सिरों पर fixed है, तो वो उस ladder का हर harmonic रखता है।
Data छोटा है — length zero point five metre, speed two hundred। बस इतना ही चाहिए।
Fundamental है v over two L, यानी two hundred over two into zero point five, जो two hundred over one, साफ़ two hundred hertz।
String सारे harmonics support करता है, तो overtones बस fundamental के अगले integer multiples हैं। कुछ skip नहीं होता।
तो first overtone fundamental का दोगुना, four hundred hertz, और second overtone उसका तीन गुना, six hundred hertz।
यहाँ vocabulary पक्की करो। String के लिए first overtone second harmonic है और second overtone third harmonic। String और open pipe कुछ skip नहीं करते।
Final answer — fundamental two hundred hertz, और first two overtones four hundred और six hundred hertz।

sections.title: Worked example: closed pipe first overtone

board_events.text: Worked example: closed pipe first overtone (NEET)

board_events.caption: The even harmonic is missing

board_events.text: A closed organ pipe has fundamental 200 Hz. Find the frequency of its first overtone.
The trap: reflexively doubling to 400 Hz. A closed pipe has NO even harmonics.
A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics: f, 3f, 5f. The first overtone is the 3rd harmonic.
First overtone jumps straight to 3 f1, skipping 2 f1 entirely.
Answer: 600 Hz.

segments.text: A short N E E T trap that catches almost everyone on autopilot. A closed organ pipe has a fundamental of two hundred hertz. What is the frequency of its first overtone?
The figure is the whole warning. The fundamental is a quarter wave, and the very next allowed pattern is three quarters of a wave. The two loop pattern in between simply is not allowed.
So the question is deceptively simple, and that is exactly the danger.

Here is the trap. Students reflexively double the fundamental to four hundred hertz, thinking first overtone means second harmonic. For a closed pipe that is flatly wrong, because even harmonics do not exist at all.
The fix is the boundary rule. A closed pipe supports only odd harmonics, f, three f, five f. So the first overtone is not the second harmonic; it is the third.
Therefore the first overtone is three times the fundamental, three times two hundred, which is six hundred hertz.
<whisper>Burn this in. In a closed pipe the first overtone leapfrogs straight to three f one, skipping two f one entirely.</whisper>
So the answer is six hundred hertz, not four hundred.
एक छोटा N E E T trap जो autopilot पर लगभग सबको पकड़ लेता है। एक closed organ pipe का fundamental two hundred hertz है। उसके first overtone की frequency क्या है?
Figure पूरी warning है। Fundamental एक quarter wave है, और अगला allowed pattern three quarters of a wave। बीच वाला two loop pattern allowed ही नहीं है।
तो सवाल धोखे से simple है, और वही ख़तरा है।

यहाँ trap है। Students reflexively fundamental को double करके four hundred hertz कर देते हैं, ये सोचकर कि first overtone यानी second harmonic। Closed pipe के लिए ये सरासर ग़लत है, क्योंकि even harmonics होते ही नहीं।
Fix boundary rule है। Closed pipe सिर्फ़ odd harmonics support करता है, f, three f, five f। तो first overtone second harmonic नहीं; third है।
<excited>इसलिए first overtone fundamental का तीन गुना, three into two hundred, यानी six hundred hertz।</excited>
इसे पक्का बिठा लो। Closed pipe में first overtone सीधे three f one पर leapfrog करता है, two f one को पूरी तरह skip करके।
तो answer है six hundred hertz, four hundred नहीं।
